errors.problem: The tap-gloss lookup ignores the harakat and matches a different vocabulary entry with the same consonant skeleton, so the learner taps the minimal-pair word and gets the meaning of its partner or of an unrelated word: ظُهْر (noon) shows 'back (of the body)' (= ظَهْر); كَاتَبَ (he corresponded) shows 'writer' (= كَاتِب); دَرَّسَ (he taught) shows 'lesson' (= دَرْس) in three places, which destroys the whole point of the shadda pair and the Form I/II rhythm page; جَمَال (beauty) shows 'camel (plural)' (= جِمَال); حَجَزَ (he booked) shows 'booking, reservation' (= حَجْز). The .en fields on the same lines are correct, so this is the engine, not the Arabic.
errors.fix: Make the tap lookup match the fully vocalised form first (or give these words their own glossary entries): ظُهْر=noon; كَاتَبَ=he corresponded with; دَرَّسَ=(he) taught; جَمَال=beauty; حَجَزَ=(he) booked
errors.alsoChange: other examples of the same mismatch in this chunk: كَاتَبَ=writer; دَرَّسَ=lesson; جَمَال=camel (plural); حَجَزَ=booking, reservation

errors.problem: هَال means cardamom (also هَيْل); 'halo' is هَالَة with tāʾ marbūṭa. The same wrong sense is repeated in the common-error text 'ḥāl (condition) and hāl (halo) sound different'. The minimal pair itself (ḥāl / hāl) is valid.
errors.alsoChange: error text → 'ḥāl (condition) and hāl (cardamom) sound different.'; the tap gloss 'هَال=halo, cardamom' → 'cardamom'

errors.current: pull the back of the tongue down and back, as if you had something hot in your mouth
errors.problem: For the emphatic ص the back of the tongue is raised and retracted (velarised/pharyngealised), as the course itself says on the emphatics page ('pull the back of your tongue up and back', 'the back of the tongue is raised towards the soft palate') and on the ṭāʾ page. This page tells the learner the opposite gesture ('down and back'), and the diagram repeats it ('pulled down and back towards the throat').
errors.fix: pull the back of the tongue up and back, as if you had something hot in your mouth
errors.alsoChange: diagram: 'for ص the back of the tongue is also pulled down and back towards the throat' → 'for ص the back of the tongue is also raised and pulled back towards the throat'

errors.problem: The transliteration engine reads a final ي / و after a long ā as a long vowel instead of a consonant: زَاي comes out as 'Zāī' and وَاو as 'Wāū'. The Arabic is right; the learner sees a letter name that contradicts the Latin name shown beside it (zāy, wāw).
errors.fix: Zāy (and Wāw for وَاو): treat ي / و after alif as consonants y / w
errors.alsoChange: the same rule produces 'Wāū' for وَاو

errors.current: Arabic never lets two consonants crash together across words.
errors.problem: Over-general rule: two consonants meet across words all the time (مِنْ مِصْر min Miṣr, عَنْ فِيلْم ʿan fīlm, both shown as pairs on this very page). The helping vowel appears only when a word ending in sukūn meets hamzat al-waṣl (al-, اِسْم …), because dropping the a of al- would leave three consonants in a row. The rest of the tip is correct.
errors.fix: Arabic never lets three consonants crash together across words.

notes.note: The darkened vowel after an emphatic is described as 'closer to the u in but' / 'the du of dull' / 'the vowel in sun or saw'. The backed a of ṣa / ḍa is nearer the a of 'father' or the o of 'hot' than the central vowel of 'but'; 'saw' is the better of the hints given. Not wrong enough to mislead, but the three pages could agree on one comparison.
'at the start of a word it carries a hamza (a glottal stop)' is a simplification: an initial alif can also be hamzat al-waṣl (اِسْم, الـ), which the wasl page later explains. Fine for day 1.

Display only: the engine renders the bare seated hamzas أ ؤ ئ as empty strings and إ as 'I', so the transliteration line reads '( i  )' and 'sit on a seat: , i,  or .'. Harmless but looks broken under the Arabic.
Same display issue: 'or as the ʿ of ع' renders as 'the ʿ of ʿ'.
ذَلِيل is 'lowly, abject, despised' rather than 'humble' (which is مُتَوَاضِع). The pair still works for the sound; a kinder gloss would be 'lowly, abject'.
Egyptian Arabic usually says 'da' for هذا rather than 'hāda'; the point about ذ → d / z is right.
مُدِير tap gloss 'director (of)' while the example gloss is 'manager'; cosmetic.
'the t is heard' before an ending is correct; it might help to add that the t is also heard before the possessive suffixes (sayyāratī, my car), which the learner meets early.
'in Lebanon and Syria a soft zh' is a fair summary; the zh is also standard in Morocco/Algeria/Tunisia, and some Gulf speakers say y. Culture note only.

The three-step stress rule is a good classroom version; it skips the detail that a final CVC syllable with a short vowel (ka-TAB-tu vs KA-tab) is not stressed. All examples given follow the rule correctly.
Tapping عَيْن on the ʿayn card shows 'eye', which is a true meaning of the word and a nice mnemonic; the other letter cards show 'the name of the letter …'. Consistency only.

summary: Checked all 31 letter entries (Latin and Arabic names, sun/moon flag, IPA, transliteration symbol, sound description, example word and gloss) and all 30 pronunciation pages (IPA, letters lists, tips, diagrams, common-error texts, examples and every minimal pair for existence, meaning and harakat). The letter data itself is clean: names, sun/moon status (14/14), IPA and symbols are all correct, and every minimal pair is a real pair with the right vowels. The one major problem is systemic, not in the content: the tap-gloss engine matches words without their harakat, so the second word of several minimal pairs shows the meaning of the first (ظُهْر = 'back', كَاتَبَ = 'writer', دَرَّسَ = 'lesson' ×3, جَمَال = 'camel (plural)', حَجَزَ = 'booking'), which teaches exactly the confusion the pages are meant to prevent. Six minor errors: هَال glossed 'halo' (it is cardamom), the sīn/ṣād page describing the emphatic tongue as pulled 'down' (the other two emphatic pages say raised), the engine transliterating زَاي / وَاو as Zāī / Wāū, the letters ل and و tapping as 'for' / 'and', context-bound tap glosses (خَيْر 'good night', سَلَام 'wow!', السَّفَر 'passport', نُور 'Nour'), and the linking page's over-general 'never two consonants across words'. Eleven notes cover vowel-comparison wording, display artefacts for seated hamzas, and a few softer glosses.
